title: Hatim Tai and His Horse
text:
Hatim al-Tai was a poet and chief of the Arab tribe of Tayy who lived in the generation before Islam, and his generosity became proverbial across the Arab and Persian world. Many stories are told of him. One of the best known concerns his horse.

Hatim owned a horse of rare beauty and speed, famous far and wide. A powerful ruler, in many versions the Byzantine emperor, heard both of the horse and of Hatim's generosity and decided to test the second by asking for the first. He sent envoys across the desert to request it.

They arrived at Hatim's tent late, in a time of drought, and he had no food to set before his guests. Rather than let them go hungry, he slaughtered the only animal he had at hand, roasted it and served it to them.

In the morning the envoys explained their mission and asked for the famous horse. Hatim told them, with sorrow, that they had eaten it the night before. He could not let guests go hungry under his roof, he said, and the horse was all he had left to give. The envoys returned and reported what had happened, and the ruler declared that Hatim's reputation fell short of the truth.
lesson: Real hospitality gives the best you have to the person in front of you, now. Do not save generosity for convenient moments.
people: Hatim al-Tai, envoys of a ruler
source: Arabic and Persian tradition on Hatim al-Tai
caveat: Hatim was a real person, but this story is a legend that exists in several versions with different rulers and details.
